agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The notes are updated, and the frozen submission C(−1.5) (14 tensors) is unchanged. This pass completes the in-sample sanity check on dev_a2, the other 256 problems of the building set. A result near or above zero would leave the overall picture as it is, a modest gain coming from freed loops. Another clearly negative result would pull the all-sets pool toward zero, and I would reconsider the submission.

On dev_a2, C(−1.5) scores −1.17 ± 1.79 (9 wrong→right, 12 right→wrong), with cut-offs again falling, 23.8% → 14.8%. All of dev_a pooled is about −1.4 ± 1.3 (20/27 over 512). All of DEV pooled is about 0 (48/49 over 1,024). HOLDOUT remains +2.2 ± 0.95 (82/55 over 1,226). Over all 2,250 practice problems, the pool is 130 wrong→right against 104 right→wrong, about +1.2 ± 0.7.

So C reliably removes about half of all cut-offs, but whether that becomes accuracy varies between sets. The HOLDOUT gain is probably at the high end of the true effect. To see why dev_a does not gain, I'll split the flips by the original's outcome, as I did for HOLDOUT. On HOLDOUT, the originally cut problems gave 35 wrong→right against 6 right→wrong, and finished problems a wash, 47 against 49. If dev_a shows the same pattern for cut problems but a net loss among finished ones, the edit's mechanism is intact and the difference is churn noise. If even the freed loops fail to gain on dev_a, the mechanism claim is weaker.

Splitting the flips by the original's outcome shows the same picture on every set:

| Set | Originally cut: wrong→right / right→wrong | Originally finished: wrong→right / right→wrong |
|---|---|---|
| HOLDOUT | 35 / 6 | 47 / 49 |
| dev_b | 17 / 1 | 11 / 21 |
| dev_a | 8 / 0 | 12 / 27 |

The loop-freeing gain is consistent on every set, about +53 net over 2,250 problems. Among problems the original finished, though, the edit costs about −27 net (70 against 97, p ≈ 0.04). That cost was hidden on HOLDOUT and visible on DEV. So C has a real side effect on answers that never looped, which matters if a cleaner variant can keep the gain without it.

C changes 14 matrices. If the loop-freeing comes mostly from one module type, attention or MLP, the other type's change may be the source of the collateral damage. First a weight statistic: the norm of the added term 1.5·‖vₗᵀW‖ for each layer and module, relative to ‖W‖. Then a log-prob statistic from passes already run (fwd_12 against fwd_8): the share of positions in originally finished answers where the original's top choice (P > 0.5) is pushed below 0.5. That gives a baseline collateral rate for C, which per-module screens could beat.

The added term is spread evenly: 4–5% of each matrix's norm, about equal for o_proj and down_proj in every layer. So the weights do not single out a dominant module. The flip proxy is informative, though. C(−1.5) pushes 0.87% of the original's confident tokens (P > 0.5) in finished answers below 0.5. That is about two to three changed choices per 300-token answer, enough to make many finished answers diverge, which fits the churn and DEV losses. C(−3) doubles the proxy to 1.9%, and the in-loop variants are much worse (3.6–6%).

So the useful measure for a cleaner variant is onset suppression per unit of flip proxy. I'll screen the two halves of C with teacher-forced passes on the same screenL texts: down_proj only first, then o_proj only. A half with most of C's onset effect (−0.44, P 0.60) but clearly less than half its flip proxy would be a candidate for a DEV generation test. If each half carries about half of each, C is as clean as this direction allows and the line closes. Plan with 10 passes: 2 screens, then a pre-registered DEV test (4 passes) against C's DEV result (48/49), then HOLDOUT only if the variant wins there.
